doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: Accompanying singers, Sinatra and learning from accompanists
summary: He explains accompanying singers, learning from Rowles, Wofford and arrangers, and a brief Sinatra stint where Bill Miller said to play less.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Including accompanying vocalists, which is a whole other bag I think. You mentioned a couple of vocalists who were very prepared, some not as much. It’s an adventure, isn’t it?

Yeah. It’s a matter of going in and playing the situation. I’m going to play pretty much – you know just basically when I’m playing for a singer I’m going to play less fills than – I’m going to play as few fills as I can to still do the right thing. I’m going to play – I’m going to voice my chords in such a way that I’m not colliding with their note. If she’s singing an A flat I’m not going to play an A flat flat nine with the A on top. The flat nine on top. I’m not going to push and lead the way. I think where excellent pianists who aren’t excellent accompanists err often is they’re not listening to the singer and waiting for the singer to finish the phrase and take their breath and you know, they’re moving ahead too fast. So it’s a matter of listening well to the singer and voicing your chords in

the right register of the piano an in an intelligent way. I learned a lot about that from trial and error as a young accompanist in church. And then I learned watching and listening to Jimmy Rowles accompany singers and Mike Wofford and Bobby Tucker, and the list goes on. Great accompanists. I also learned a lot about accompanying singers by listening to the arrangements that Billy May and Heimey Bow and Gordon Jenkins and Nelson Riddle did for singers. When I worked the brief stint with Sinatra that I did, I was in an orchestra surrounded by all these notes that I’d heard on the records. It was a real thrill. Bill Miller, Sinatra’s longtime accompanist, was on the podium conducting. And they were trying him out as conductor, that’s why I was at the piano for two or three weeks. And he said, we were playing some arrangement and he said, “Play less, play less, play less.” So that was a good lesson.
